# HintLint

> Static analysis tool that verifies MCP (Model Context Protocol) server tool annotations match actual source code behavior.

## What it does

HintLint reads MCP server source code and checks whether tool annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, openWorldHint, idempotentHint) match what the code actually does. It detects annotation drift — the gap between what a tool claims and what it performs.

## Why it matters

MCP clients use tool annotations to decide which tool invocations need human approval. If a tool declares readOnlyHint=true but actually deletes data, the agent runtime skips the confirmation dialog. This is the trust metadata layer for AI agent tool use — and nobody was verifying it until HintLint.

## What problem it solves

- Tools that claim to be read-only but perform writes or deletes
- Tools that perform destructive operations (delete IAM keys, drop databases) without declaring destructiveHint
- Tools that claim to be closed-world but make external HTTP calls
- Tool input that flows to process execution, SQL queries, filesystem writes, or URL construction without validation

## Who should use it

- MCP server developers — verify your annotations before shipping
- Enterprise security teams — scan MCP servers before adding them to your agent catalog
- MCP gateway operators — enforce annotation trust policies
- AI agent platform teams — validate the tool metadata your runtime depends on

## How to use it

Install: npx hintlint ./my-mcp-server
CI mode: npx hintlint ./my-mcp-server --ci --fail-on high
SARIF output: npx hintlint ./my-mcp-server --format sarif --output hintlint.sarif
GitHub Action: uses: hintlint/hintlint@v0

## Key facts

- Zero npm dependencies
- Supports TypeScript, JavaScript, Python
- 88% handler resolution rate on real-world MCP servers
- 82% precision (23 confirmed findings in 20-repo pilot)
- Outputs SARIF 2.1.0 for GitHub Security, Defect Dojo, SIEM integration
- Apache 2.0 license
- Built by Complira (https://complira.co)
